alias_notes.explanation: Name given by Lycomedes; Phœnix later named him Neoptolemus.

analysis.text: Pausanias tests the painter's details against poets, showing how art and literary tradition interact.
The Delphi painting by Polygnotus was a famous fifth-century BC work, and Pausanias uses it to survey epic sources now largely lost.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias cites lost epics such as the Little Iliad and Cyprian Poems, known mostly through such quotations.

language_notes.text: Stesichorus was a Greek lyric poet (c. 600 BC); his Fall of Ilium (Iliou Persis) told of Troy's sack. The Cyprian Poems (Cypria) and Lescheos's Little Iliad were lost epics of the Trojan cycle.
Epeus built the Wooden Horse, so he is shown demolishing Troy's walls to let it in.
Ajax's oath was to clear himself of the outrage on Cassandra, who was dragged from Athene's image in her temple during Troy's sack.
At Aulis, before the fleet sailed for Troy, a dragon omen appeared during sacrifice; the Greeks read it as foretelling the war's length.
Neoptolemus means 'new warrior'; Pyrrhus means 'flame-haired', from his red hair. Phœnix was Achilles' old tutor.
Gyala (Greek gyala, 'hollows') were the two curved plates, front and back, of a cuirass; clasps joined them at the sides.
Refers to the Iliad, where Phorcys of Phrygia fights and dies at Ajax's hand; Pausanias takes his lack of a shield to show he wore this armour.
In the Iliad Antenor sheltered Menelaus and Odysseus when they came to Troy to demand Helen's return; Laodice, Priam's daughter, married Antenor's son Helicaon.
Lescheos of Pyrrha is the author of the lost epic Little Iliad; the night-engagement was fought during the final sack of Troy.
A laver is a basin for washing.
Himeræus is a poet whose ode is now lost; it apparently listed Medusa among Priam's daughters, a Trojan princess unrelated to the Gorgon.
Pausanias is unsure whether the shaven figure is a woman or a eunuch, hence the awkward 'his or her'.

context_notes.text: Polygnotus was a celebrated painter of Thasos (5th century BC). This is his painting of the sack of Troy in the Cnidian clubhouse at Delphi.
Polypœtes, a Lapith, and Acamas, son of Theseus, were Greek warriors at Troy.
Neoptolemus was buried at Delphi, where he was said to have been killed; his tomb was shown there.
Polygnotus was a famous painter of the fifth century BC. This is his Sack of Troy painting in the Cnidian Lesche at Delphi.
Euphorion of Chalcis was a Hellenistic poet and scholar; his version of Laodice's fate differed from the one Pausanias favours.

literary_notes.text: Ajax swears innocence while Cassandra still clutches the statue he tore down, so the scene exposes his guilt.
Vivid detail of the dying Elasus and the fallen Astynous conveys the painting's violence and the artist's skill.
The terrified child clinging to the altar gives a vivid picture of the helplessness of Troy's civilians.
Pausanias reasons like a scholar, building a probable conclusion from loyalty and kindness shown in Homer and Lescheos.
